whoIsThisFor.heading: Who should take the B2B Solution Architect exam?

personas.label: Cross-cloud practitioners
personas.description: You have delivered Salesforce solutions for B2B businesses and want to show that you can design across clouds and connected systems.

personas.label: Solution designers
personas.description: You lead discovery and design for projects that connect Salesforce clouds with ERP, billing, warehouse, or other platforms.

personas.label: Consultants moving into architecture
personas.description: You have focused on one cloud and are ready to plan the full B2B process across teams and systems.

examDifficulty.heading: How challenging is the B2B Solution Architect exam?
examDifficulty.summary: This exam covers a wide range of B2B design decisions. One question may focus on data shared across clouds, another on ERP integration, and another on delivery practices. Project experience helps you apply the concepts to business needs.
bullets: 60 scored questions in 120 minutes, plus up to five unscored questions that do not count.
58% to pass, which is 35 correct answers out of 60.
Cross-cloud situations: Questions may combine Sales Cloud, Service Cloud, CPQ, Order Management, B2B Commerce, and Experience Cloud.
Delivery practices matter: Prepare for questions about discovery, governance, and user adoption as well as technology.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: Experience designing B2B solutions can help. Before booking, aim for 75% or more on practice tests and be ready to explain how a quote, order, invoice, and service request move across the systems in your design.

examFormat.heading: B2B Solution Architect exam format
examFormat.intro: You can take the exam online with a proctor or at a test center. Expect scenarios about business processes and system design.
examFormat.scenarioPercent: Many questions describe a B2B company with a problem such as slow quoting or customer data split across systems. Choose the design that addresses the stated need and assigns clear ownership.
bestWayToPass: Trace the full B2B process: Understand how lead, opportunity, quote, order, fulfillment, invoice, and service fit together, and which system handles each step.
Set data ownership: Identify the source of truth for accounts, products, prices, and orders before designing synchronization.
Choose the integration pattern: Use real-time requests when a user needs an answer now, events when systems need to know about a change, and batch jobs for large scheduled loads.
Prepare for delivery questions: Review discovery, requirements, design governance, release planning, and adoption.

certificationCard.description: This exam tests how you design B2B solutions that span several Salesforce clouds and outside systems. You decide where data lives, how systems connect, and how the project is run.

keyConcepts.h2: B2B Solution Architect exam: key concepts

blocks.heading: Solution Architecture Fundamentals
blocks.body: Start with the business process and its problems, then choose the products and systems that support each step. A common B2B flow uses Sales Cloud for leads and opportunities, CPQ or Revenue Cloud for quotes, Order Management or an ERP for orders, an ERP for invoicing, and Service Cloud for support. Experience Cloud or B2B Commerce can give customers and partners self-service access. Prefer standard features and configuration when they meet the need; custom code adds work to maintain and upgrade.

blocks.heading: Multi-Cloud Data Architecture
blocks.body: Each important record should have a clear **source of truth**. For example, Salesforce may own customer accounts while an ERP owns products and prices, with those details synchronized into Salesforce for quoting. Orders may begin in Salesforce and continue in the ERP. Use **external IDs** to match records across systems and keep the shared Account and Contact model clear. Plan for large order and asset volumes, including archiving. **Data Cloud** can combine customer information from several sources into unified profiles without copying every record into core CRM objects.

blocks.heading: Integration Architecture Patterns
blocks.body: Most B2B designs connect Salesforce to an ERP. Use a real-time API request when someone is waiting for an answer, such as a stock or credit check during quoting. Use **Platform Events** or **Change Data Capture** to notify other systems that something changed. Use a batch process and Bulk API for large scheduled transfers, such as nightly price updates. When several systems need connections, middleware such as MuleSoft can organize and reuse those integrations.

blocks.heading: Security & Compliance Design
blocks.body: Customers and partners may use an Experience Cloud site to access Salesforce. Set sharing so each company sees only its own accounts, orders, and cases; account relationships and sharing sets can support external access. Consider data residency, consent, and privacy rules such as GDPR when personal data moves between countries or systems. Single sign-on can simplify access for employees and partners. Regulated businesses may also need Shield encryption or Event Monitoring.

blocks.heading: Governance, Change Management & Scalability
blocks.body: Large B2B projects involve many groups, so agree on how design decisions are made. A design authority, shared naming and coding standards, and a release plan help teams stay aligned. Run business discovery before settling on a solution. Plan training and adoption early so people can use the new system. Design with expected growth in users, orders, and markets in mind.

scenarioTips.h2: How to prepare for the B2B Solution Architect exam
scenarioTips.intro: Each scenario gives a business need and several possible designs. Choose an option that solves the stated problem, uses clear ownership for data, and avoids custom work when a standard approach fits.

blocks.heading: B2B Process Design
blocks.body: Map each process step to the cloud or system responsible for it. Look for the step where the business is experiencing a delay or error.

blocks.heading: Shared Data Model
blocks.body: Keep a consistent Account and Contact model. Decide which system owns products, prices, and orders, then use external IDs to link records.

blocks.heading: Integration Choices
blocks.body: Use real-time calls when a person is waiting, events to notify other systems of changes, and batch processing for large scheduled transfers. Consider middleware as systems multiply.

blocks.heading: Quoting and Commerce
blocks.body: Know how CPQ or Revenue Cloud supports quotes and how approved quotes become orders. Identify where price rules live and how orders reach the ERP.

blocks.heading: Customer Self-Service
blocks.body: Use Experience Cloud or B2B Commerce when customers and partners need to check orders, cases, or invoices without contacting support.

nextCertsAfter.heading: Next Architect Certifications
nextCertsAfter.intro: After B2B Solution Architect, many people move toward the platform architect credentials and CTA:

sampleQuestions.question: Sales reps wait two days for quotes because finance keeps pricing rules in spreadsheets. What should the architect recommend?
options: Build a custom component that reads the spreadsheet for every quote
Move pricing and discount rules into CPQ with approval steps
Hire more finance staff to answer quote requests
Send the spreadsheet to sales reps each week
sampleQuestions.explanation: Putting prices, discounts, and approval rules in CPQ lets reps create quotes with current rules and route exceptions for review.
whyWrong: Reading spreadsheets from custom code on every quote adds fragile work and leaves the pricing process unchanged.
More staff may reduce a queue but does not give reps a managed quoting process.
Weekly spreadsheets can become stale and do not enforce approvals in the quote flow.

sampleQuestions.question: The ERP owns product and price data, but sales reps create quotes in Salesforce. How should the architect handle that data?
options: Let reps edit Salesforce prices and copy changes back to the ERP
Keep the ERP as the source of truth and sync the data into Salesforce
Require reps to check each price in the ERP while quoting
Keep two price lists and let reps decide which one to use
sampleQuestions.explanation: The ERP owns these records, so Salesforce should receive synchronized data for quoting rather than becoming a second owner.
whyWrong: Allowing edits in both systems creates conflicting values and unclear ownership.
Manual lookups slow quoting and can still lead to entry errors.
Two lists create uncertainty about which price is valid.

sampleQuestions.question: While preparing a quote, a rep must check current ERP stock before promising a delivery date. Which integration pattern fits?
options: Real-time ERP stock check
Publish a Platform Event after the quote is saved
Use the previous night’s stock batch
Send a weekly stock export to Salesforce
sampleQuestions.explanation: The rep needs current stock before making a commitment, so a synchronous request and response fits the decision.
whyWrong: An event after saving the quote does not return stock while the rep is making the decision.
Nightly data may be too old for a live availability check.
A weekly export is even less current and cannot answer the immediate question.

sampleQuestions.question: The ERP, billing platform, warehouse, and data lake all need to know when Salesforce places an order. What should the architect use?
options: Send each system a nightly CSV file
Add four separate callouts to the order trigger
Publish an event when the order is placed
Have each system poll Salesforce every minute
sampleQuestions.explanation: One order event can notify multiple subscribers. New systems can listen without adding another direct call to the order transaction.
whyWrong: A nightly file delays notification and may not meet downstream needs.
Four synchronous callouts couple the order transaction to every receiver.
Frequent polling adds load and makes every receiving system manage its own checks.

sampleQuestions.question: Partner companies use Experience Cloud to view their orders. What is the key security design requirement?
options: Restrict each partner to its own account’s records
Limit how many reports partners can run
Use the internal users’ page layout for every partner
Choose a different color scheme for each company
sampleQuestions.explanation: External sharing must keep each partner’s accounts and orders private from other companies.
whyWrong: Report limits do not define which records a partner can access.
Page layouts control fields and presentation, not record-level access.
Brand colors do not enforce data separation.

sampleQuestions.question: Customer details are spread across Salesforce, an ERP, a marketing system, and support software. The core org should not hold all source records. What can provide a unified customer view?
options: Ask staff to update all four systems by hand
Use Data Cloud to unify customer profiles from the sources
Delete all but one of the source systems
Copy every source record into custom CRM objects
sampleQuestions.explanation: Data Cloud can bring data from multiple sources together into unified profiles without requiring every record to be stored in core CRM objects.
whyWrong: Manual updates are costly and can leave the systems inconsistent.
Removing systems does not address the need to use their business functions and data.
Copying all source data into custom objects would add the storage burden the company wants to avoid.

sampleQuestions.question: Where should an architect begin when planning a new B2B solution?
options: Map the process and pain points
Design the page layouts
Write the integration code
Choose Salesforce licenses
sampleQuestions.explanation: Understanding the process and its problems helps determine which capabilities and systems are needed.
whyWrong: Page layouts come after the user and process needs are understood.
Integration code depends on decisions about the process and systems.
Licensing should follow the solution requirements, not drive discovery.

sampleQuestions.question: Salesforce captures an order, the ERP fulfills it, and billing creates the invoice. What design principle helps keep the process clear?
options: Re-enter the order by hand in each system
Keep order information only in Salesforce
Give each step a clear owning system
Let every system edit every order field
sampleQuestions.explanation: Clear ownership for each step reduces conflicting updates and makes the order easier to trace across systems.
whyWrong: Manual re-entry increases delay and data entry errors.
The ERP and billing system also need the order data to complete their work.
Allowing all systems to change every field creates conflicts over which value is correct.

sampleQuestions.question: A global B2B company handles personal data for customers in the EU. What must the architect include in the design?
options: Website performance alone
The number of user licenses alone
The interface language only
Privacy requirements such as GDPR
sampleQuestions.explanation: The solution must account for privacy obligations, including consent, data access requests, and where personal data is stored and processed.
whyWrong: Performance alone does not address legal handling of personal data.
License counts do not determine privacy controls.
Language settings do not satisfy privacy requirements.

sampleQuestions.question: Six delivery teams are making conflicting architecture choices. What governance step should the architect recommend?
options: Allow each team to set its own standards
Set up a design authority and shared standards
Stop all but one team from working
Combine all work into one annual release
sampleQuestions.explanation: A design authority and shared standards help teams make consistent decisions while continuing work in parallel.
whyWrong: Independent standards can increase inconsistency across teams.
Stopping all but one team unnecessarily blocks parallel delivery.
One annual release can delay value and does not resolve design decisions during delivery.

sampleQuestions.question: Customers call support to ask about order status and download invoices. What solution could reduce these calls?
options: Email each customer a spreadsheet every week
Hire more support agents
Close the support phone line
Provide a self-service portal for orders and invoices
sampleQuestions.explanation: A portal through Experience Cloud or B2B Commerce lets customers find order and invoice information themselves.
whyWrong: Weekly spreadsheets become outdated and make customers depend on staff.
More agents address call volume without letting customers self-serve.
Closing the support line removes help instead of solving the information need.

sampleQuestions.question: A sponsor requests a custom quoting engine, but standard CPQ meets 90% of the requirements. What should the architect recommend?
options: Use standard CPQ and extend it for remaining needs
Delay the project for a year in case new features arrive
Run two quoting tools side by side
Build a separate custom quoting engine
sampleQuestions.explanation: Standard CPQ covers most of the need. A limited extension or process adjustment is usually simpler to maintain than a separate engine.
whyWrong: Waiting does not address the remaining requirement or provide a current solution.
Two tools create duplicate processes and make quote management harder.
A separate engine adds cost and ongoing maintenance for needs mostly covered by CPQ.

sampleQuestions.question: The ERP sends a nightly price update for 200,000 products. Which approach is suitable?
options: Make one real-time callout per product
Publish a Platform Event for every product
Use a batch load with Bulk API
Ask the product team to enter every price manually
sampleQuestions.explanation: Bulk API is designed to move large data volumes efficiently in scheduled loads.
whyWrong: A separate real-time call for every item adds avoidable overhead.
An event for each product is not the best fit for a large nightly bulk transfer.
Manual entry is too slow and error-prone at this scale.

sampleQuestions.question: A solution launched six months ago, but few sales reps use it. What was likely missing?
options: Add more custom code to the solution
Add more page fields for the sales reps
Increase the sandbox capacity for the project
Plan training and adoption
sampleQuestions.explanation: Users need preparation and support to adopt a new process. Adoption planning should begin during delivery.
whyWrong: More code does not address whether users understand or accept the process.
Adding fields can make the experience more complex without helping adoption.
A larger sandbox does not improve user readiness.

sampleQuestions.question: The same customer exists in Salesforce and the ERP, but each system uses a different record ID. How should integrations match the records?
options: Match them by customer name during nightly processing
Ask users to connect the records manually
Store the ERP key in Salesforce as an external ID
Keep the records unrelated
sampleQuestions.explanation: An external ID stores the other system’s key so integrations can reliably match and upsert the same customer.
whyWrong: Names can change or be shared by different customers, so they are not a reliable key.
Manual linking does not scale and can lead to mismatches.
Leaving records unrelated makes synchronization and reporting harder.
